term: Draw the light, not the asset
meaning: His most common note to background artists: an asset isn't finished when it's modeled and textured with base colors; it must express the light it reflects in its environment.
Sakurai's name for the visual flair shown when an attack connects (sparks, flashes, shockwaves); guard effects count as hit marks too.
His name for the effect left behind by a sword swing, usually a fading polygon ribbon, sometimes a one-frame flat image; he's not sure there's a universal term.
His term for making the screen or a character shine: a full-screen flash for impact, a character flash to emphasize a change in status.
An effect 'pops' when it has impact and contrast against any background, achieved with crisp shapes and dark elements rather than additive brightness alone.
Adding an element's colors to the background so the result moves toward white; distinct from translucency, which moves toward the element's own colors. Useful but not enough on its own.
Polygons or simple images mixed into an effect and made its focus, giving Smash Ultimate's effects a clean, anime-style look.

term: A fight between live action and animation
meaning: What a cast or world looks like when realistic and cartoony designs are dropped together unadjusted; his shorthand for a failure of style unification.
A few pieces of art by an exceptional artist showing a game's world, scenery, characters and items, used as the reference that unifies the team's style.
Whether an object or effect reads at its intended size; CG objects tend to look like scale models, and big things looking too small is the usual failure.
The finished frame after everything is drawn into the framebuffer and post-processed; on powerful hardware it matters more than any single model.
His umbrella word for everything (visuals, audio, programming, parameters) that together makes a massless game world feel real.
How much an environment object means to the player, which comes from gameplay (cautious, high-death play makes players scrutinize everything) rather than from the art alone.
His description of game worlds from a creator's view: decoration without mass or collision until gameplay and programming give it substance.
The distinction between the parts of the screen that have more or less impact on players, used to decide where limited performance and labor go.
The way distant things lose contrast and saturation and take on atmospheric color; used to push backdrops back and to make big things read as big.
Differences in how each monitor (and room lighting) shows the same color, which he treats as fatal for art reviews.
Lighting that looks like it shines from behind a character, emphasizing the outline; Smash Ultimate uses it for certain damage types and statuses such as invulnerability.
A flat object, usually a two-polygon mesh, that always faces the camera; cheap to render and ideal for particles and light flashes. A Y-axis billboard turns only around the vertical axis.
The draw order that decides whether characters or effects appear in front; easy to force in 2D, but forcing it in 3D causes depth disparity.
A quick paintover of an artist's own work, five to ten minutes in his case, sent beside the original to show direction rather than describe it.
A simulation filter (now built into Photoshop) that shows how art looks with types of color blindness such as protanopia; he used it to check Meteos.
